data: West Asia and the Mediterranean 200-700 CE: Empires, Religions and Replacement

The early centuries of the Common Era in West Asia are dominated in historiography by two opposed empires, that of the Romans and that of the Persians. Arguably the whole of European history, which has subsequently been exported to much of the globe, is the process of dealing with and occasionally trying to reverse the end of the Roman culture; Persia, though less well-recorded, is no less significant for its inheritors, Islamic and otherwise. This course charts the entwined fates of the two empires in their long final phase, which ended with their replacement, in whole or in part, by a new competitor in the form of the first Islamic caliphate. Religion, ethnic identity and ideas about power come to the fore in this course, which will leave you understanding better both the shape of the world which West Asia has affected today and the enduring cultural significance of Rome, and Persia, as archetypes and aspirations.
